sections.history: Tiruveezhimizhalai is an ancient Shaiva village-temple in the delta country near Needamangalam, counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams and hymned by Sambandar, Appar and Sundarar. The stone temple carries Chola-period workmanship with later additions, but its fame rests less on its fabric than on the events of the Tevaram age, when the two great saints are said to have sheltered here during a famine and fed the people by the lord's gift.
sections.architecture: The temple follows the Dravidian plan with a gopuram, pillared halls and a sanctum enshrining the lingam of Veezhinathar; the goddess Sundarakuchambikai has her own shrine. Within the complex, tradition points to the seats where the two saints are said to have received their daily gold coin — one near the maha-mandapam and another toward the western side — so that the great famine miracle is tied to specific places a pilgrim can still stand before.
sections.legends: The defining legend is the famine of the Tevaram age. With the land starving and the saints without means, Sambandar and Appar prayed to Veezhinathar, and each was granted a gold coin — the padikasu — every morning. One telling adds that the coins given to the younger Sambandar were of lower value than Appar's, and that Sambandar sang a hymn appealing to the lord, after which the coins were made equal. Unable to bear the people's suffering, the saints set up feeding houses and distributed food until the famine passed.
sections.festivals: The temple observes the Shaiva festivals — Maha Shivaratri, the Margazhi hymn-singing, Pradosham and the annual Brahmotsavam. The memory of the padikasu miracle gives the temple a special association with annadanam, the giving of food, and acts of charity are considered especially fitting here.
sections.experience: Tiruveezhimizhalai is a quiet delta temple whose power lies in its story. Pilgrims come knowing the tale of the gold coins and the fed multitude, and standing at the saints' seats they feel the nearness of a grace that answered hunger with generosity. It is a place that joins devotion to the simple, human act of feeding others.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer corridors but not inside the sanctum; ask temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Tiruveezhimizhalai is near Needamangalam in Tiruvarur district, roughly 20 km from Tiruvarur and about 15 km from Kumbakonam; the nearest rail heads are Needamangalam and Kumbakonam, with buses and taxis to the village.
